one_liner: Measure how far a point is from the origin along all directions.
everyday: Imagine you're standing in a city with a grid of streets. Your friend is 3 blocks east and 4 blocks north of you. How far away are they? You could count the total blocks walked on sidewalks (7 blocks), or you could measure the straight-line distance by walking diagonally. The straight-line distance is shorter — about 5 blocks. A norm does the same thing for lists of numbers: it gives you a single distance measurement from a starting point.

In machine learning, models often produce lists of numbers called vectors — maybe a list of features, or the outputs from each node in a network layer. We need a single number that tells us how large or significant that whole list is. Is this vector small and near zero, or huge and far away? A norm gives us that single summary number. It captures magnitude in a way that works no matter how many dimensions you have.
symbols: The L2 norm of vector x — the straight-line distance from the origin to the point x in space.
A vector, which is a list of numbers arranged in order (like [3, 4] for the city example).

worked.title: Finding the distance of a point in 2D space
lines: Vector x = [3, 4] (3 units east, 4 units north)
So ||x||_2 = 5 (the point is 5 units away from the origin)

matters: Norms show up everywhere in machine learning because models constantly need to measure how far vectors have moved, how large their outputs are, or how different two vectors are from each other. When training a neural network, we measure how wrong the predictions are by taking norms of error vectors. When checking if a model has learned to be sparse (using only a few important features), we measure the L1 norm, which counts the total absolute magnitude. When constraining a model to be stable or interpretable, we often limit how large certain weight vectors can get — a limit on their norm. Across the 122 papers that use this idea, norms appear in optimization (measuring progress), in safety checks (bounding model behavior), and in representation learning (comparing how similar two learned vectors are).

The L2 norm specifically is like the straight-line distance you learned in math class — it squares each component, sums them, then takes the square root. This works because the Pythagorean theorem tells us that if you move 3 units in one direction and 4 in another, the straight-line distance is the square root of 3 squared plus 4 squared, which is 5. So the L2 norm directly answers the question 'how far away is this point?' in real geometric space. The L1 norm is the taxicab distance — just add up the absolute values of all components, like counting city blocks instead of walking diagonally. Different norms are useful for different jobs: L2 for measuring smooth distances and checking size, L1 for finding sparse solutions where most numbers are zero.
